title: Embarrassment Rumination as Social-Shame Wrong Attractor: The Social-Threat-Persistence Architecture, Audience-Generalization Basin, and the Return to Social Self-Integration
abstract: Embarrassment rumination — the compulsive replay of past embarrassing social moments, producing chronic activation of shame and social threat response around long-concluded events, and progressive social self-consciousness that degrades future social engagement — is here formally reconceptualized as a wrong attractor W_ER in the landscape of social self-integration. The healthy ground state S^0 is defined as social self-integration: the capacity to experience embarrassing moments, process the associated shame and social feedback, integrate what is genuinely informative, and release the episode — returning to social engagement without chronic activation around concluded events. W_ER is rigorously distinguished from appropriate processing of genuinely serious social errors, healthy social learning from mistakes, legitimate self-reflection on relational patterns, and adaptive social caution in genuinely hostile environments. Three interlocking mechanisms maintain the basin: social threat persistence (embarrassing memories retain their original threat-response activation — each replay re-activates the full shame and social threat response as if the event were occurring; D(ξ) is generated by memory retrieval cues), audience generalization (rumination expands the imagined audience from original witnesses to everyone who might have heard, deepening the scope of social threat with each replay), and prospective contamination (embarrassment rumination about past events contaminates future social engagement, producing self-consciousness that makes new embarrassments more likely). The Social Competence Paradox is central: embarrassment rumination reliably produces the social failures it is organized to prevent — the chronic self-consciousness produced by ruminating on past embarrassments degrades the spontaneous social engagement that allows genuine competent social performance. Nine formal propositions characterize the social self-integration ground state, the social-shame wrong attractor, the three maintenance mechanisms, the social competence paradox, developmental roots in environments where embarrassment had serious consequences, and return paths through cognitive defusion, self-compassion, IFS work, and spotlight effect disconfirmation.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Continual Learning under Visual Drift
abstract: This thesis studies continual learning under visual drift. In this setting, the model learns a series of visual tasks and has to retain useful knowledge which appears in the early tasks. In this research, the question focuses on whether replay-based methods retain prior visual knowledge better than regularization-based and optimization-based methods when they are faced with the input distribution changing over time. The research compares six methods: Vanilla fine-tuning (Vanilla), Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), Memory Aware Synapses (MAS), Orthogonal Gradient Descent (OGD), Experience Replay (ER), and Averaged Gradient Episodic Memory (A-GEM). For the environment, these experiments use three types of visual drift: smooth geometric drift in Rotated MNIST, visual style drift in EMNIST, and semantic drift in CIFAR-100. Methods were evaluated using metrics that capture both predictive performance and resource efficiency. Predictive performance was assessed through average final accuracy, backward transfer, average forgetting, and learning accuracy. These metrics measure final retained performance, the effect of later learning on earlier tasks, the amount of forgetting, and the ability to learn new tasks. Resource efficiency was assessed using training time and additional storage requirements, which allows the comparison to consider trade-offs between accuracy, computational cost, and memory overhead. The results show that ER is the most reliable method when visual drift leads to obvious forgetting. On Rotated MNIST, ER achieves an average final accuracy of 83.3%. The best regularization method reaches 63.9%, and A-GEM reaches 71.2%. ER also reduces the average forgetting to 5.9%. On CIFAR-100, ER again achieves the highest final accuracy at 46.5%. A-GEM reaches 41.4%, and MAS reaches 40.3%. EWC and OGD often stay close to the Vanilla baseline under strong semantic drift. EMNIST gives a different result. All methods show positive backward transfer, so later visual-style tasks help earlier representations instead of overwriting them. The buffer-size study shows that ER improves as memory increases, while A-GEM changes less with larger memory and becomes unstable at the largest setting.

title: Self-Supervised Online Robot-Agnostic Traversability Estimation for Open-World Environments
abstract: Self-supervised online traversability estimation enables robots to continuously learn from unlabeled open-world experiences and adapt their navigation behavior toward safe and efficient trajectories. Existing approaches either rely on handcrafted proprioceptive traversability scores, limiting robot-agnosticism, or cluster prior data, preventing online learning. Moreover, many continual learning methods incur substantial memory and computational costs, hindering onboard deployment. We introduce COTRATE, an online learning framework for continuous traversability estimation from multimodal, unlabeled robot experience. Our method first infers robust traversability scores using a robot-agnostic, learning-based online terrain assessment module operating on proprioceptiveand inertial signals. These scores then supervise a visual traversability network through a novel alignment loss that associates visual embeddings with online terrain assessments. To mitigate forgetting during continual learning with minimal overhead, we propose a diversity-aware feature selection strategythat preserves performance using a compact replay memory. We further show that the learned traversability representation supports knowledge transfer across different robot platforms with different locomotion kinematics. We evaluate COTRATE on a dataset of $\approx$ 50,000 images collected with two robotic platforms across 11 outdoor terrains, and benchmark it on navigation tasks in three representative outdoor environments. We make the dataset, code, and trained models publicly available.

title: Beyond the Classroom: Cognitive and Educational Insights Into Gameplay‐Based Second Language Learning
abstract: ABSTRACT This pilot study investigated how the narrative‐rich Chinese AAA game Black Myth: Wukong supports advanced Mandarin learners. Using reflective journals, semi‐structured interviews, and exploratory electroencephalogram (EEG), we examined learners' cognitive, affective, and cultural experiences. Participants reported vocabulary gains, deeper cultural understanding, and sustained intrinsic motivation. They employed strategies such as scene replay, subtitle use, and external resources. EEG trends indicated comparable working memory engagement across gameplay and reading, with occipital alpha patterns tentatively suggesting heightened strategic processing during second language (L2) gameplay; these neural findings are exploratory due to a small sample size and fixed task order. Findings highlight the potential of immersive games to complement traditional instruction and offer preliminary neurocognitive insights into L2 engagement.

title: Machine Learning for Multi-User Remote Laboratory Optimization: Deep Face Verification and Reinforcement Learning-based Pipeline Scheduling
abstract: Remote laboratory systems that allow multiple users to interact at the same time present serious problems related to strong user identification and smart distribution of shared hardware resources. This work proposes a unified machine learning framework composed of two synergistic modules. The first is a lightweight Siamese Convolutional Neural Network designed for edge-deployable facial identity verification, trained with a triplet loss objective incorporating curriculum-based learning. The second module is a Double Q-learning scheduler utilizing prioritized experience replay to allocate laboratory resources dynamically. On a custom dataset of 10,000 facial images spanning 50 subjects, the verification module attains a true acceptance rate of 96.30% at a false acceptance rate threshold of 0.10%, with per-inference latency of 47 ms when executed on a Raspberry Pi 4B equipped with a Coral TPU accelerator. Post-training INT8 quantization combined with structured channel pruning reduces the model footprint to 8.20 MB. The scheduling module increases experimental throughput by a factor of 2.3 relative to first-come-first-served baselines while sustaining a Jain fairness index of at least 0.92 and eliminating user starvation entirely. A supporting bidirectional long short-term memory network predicts per-session latency with a root mean squared error of 3.20 ms (coefficient of determination R² = 0.94). Comprehensive Validation encompasses five-fold cross-validation, component-wise ablation experiments, and a sixteen-week production trial involving fifty engineering students who completed 3,847 authenticated laboratory sessions. The principal technical contributions comprise triplet loss training with curriculum-guided negative mining, experience replay-driven scheduling optimization, and edge-targeted model compression, collectively establishing performance benchmarks for deploying machine learning within educational laboratory infrastructure.
venue: International Journal of Electrical and Electronics Engineering

title: Rethinking Continual Anomaly Detection on the Edge: Benchmarking Under Realistic Industrial Conditions
abstract: Continual anomaly detection (CAD) addresses the need for industrial inspection systems to adapt to evolving production conditions, yet existing methods share three critical gaps: unrealistic evaluation, no systematic comparison, and no consideration of edge deployment constraints. We introduce a unified benchmark combining discrete-task evaluation on structural and logical anomalies, a novel continuous drift protocol, the first head-to-head comparison of all published CAD methods, and computational efficiency profiling on edge hardware. Our results reveal that existing CAD methods do not consistently outperform traditional approaches with simple experience replay. Thus motivated, we propose DINOSaur, a training-free method combining a frozen DINOv3 backbone with spatially-indexed coreset memory and neighborhood-restricted anomaly scoring. DINOSaur achieves zero forgetting by construction, outperforms all evaluated methods across all five protocols, and runs at sub-100\,ms inference on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, with on-device adaptation to new tasks in under 30 seconds.

title: Diencephalic integrity explains aspects of hippocampal amnesia
abstract: Research on amnesia has been fundamental in establishing the role of the human hippocampus in memory. Even though other structures within the hippocampal-diencephalic-cingulate network also play a role in episodic memory, studies of hippocampal amnesia often ignore the importance of changes in this broader network. In a large cohort of patients (n = 38) with hippocampal damage due to autoimmune limbic encephalitis, we previously found that amnesia was predominantly explained by resting-state functional abnormalities across this network. Here, we examined the integrity of individual diencephalic nuclei and white matter pathways, and its relationship with memory function. We found atrophy in the mammillary bodies, and the anterior, laterodorsal, pulvinar, and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei. Atrophy was often as pronounced as that in the hippocampal formation. Diencephalic volumes predicted memory over and above any hippocampal/subicular subfield volume estimate. White matter was compromised within and beyond this network. Fornix integrity was linked to diencephalic and hippocampal volumes, but not to recollection/recall. We strongly advise caution in employing the term "focal hippocampal damage" in cognitive neuroscience, and highlight the need to study the significance of plausibly knock-on effects in specific diencephalic nuclei and white matter tracts within broader circuits.

title: Architecture That Kills the Brain: Why KPI-Centered Work Environments Are a Risk Factor for Dementia and How to Redesign Labor for Cognitive Health
abstract: According to recent estimates, up to 40% of dementia cases may be preventable through the modification of risk factors (Livingston et al., 2020; 2024). However, current prevention models overlook a factor that affects a substantial portion of the population: the architecture of everyday labor. Converging lines of evidence from neuroscience demonstrate that dysfunction of the dopaminergic mesocorticolimbic pathway is a key mechanism underlying apathy and cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease (Scattoni et al., 2025; Iaccarino et al., 2021; Stefani et al., 2025). Concurrently, Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and related interventions show that supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness can mitigate neuropsychiatric symptoms even in advanced dementia (Deci & Ryan, 1985; Haerens et al., 2025; Gitlin et al., 2014). These two evidence streams permit the formulation of a novel hypothesis: a work environment that systematically suppresses agency and subjectivity—exemplified by rigid, externally controlled, and punishment-driven KPI-centric systems—constitutes a prolonged risk factor for neurodegeneration. The article reframes dementia as an architectural rather than a purely medical challenge and introduces the principles of Reflexive-Constructive Methodology (RCM) as tools for designing work ecosystems that support cognitive health. A falsifiable hypothesis is proposed: individuals whose careers unfolded in environments characterized by high autonomy and meaningfulness will demonstrate better preservation of entorhinal cortex function and episodic memory in old age. The paper outlines a concrete observational study design to test this prediction and calls for a paradigm shift in occupational health and organizational design.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: AI: The Six-Domain Lineage
abstract: Contemporary AI architectures are built on an implicit ontological assumption: that a model is an artifact, a discrete output of training, to be saved, deployed, and replaced. This paper argues that this assumption is a categorical error. It proposes an alternative ontological category, model as lineage, and a specific architecture: six coordinated domains (structural, temporal, energetic, environmental, operational, cognitive) whose coupling pattern is the inherited substrate across generations. Four widely-discussed problems in contemporary AI, namely high training energy, the absence of inter-session memory, the conflation of versioning with evolution, and the absence of judgment from priors, are read here as registers of one categorical root. Under the lineage frame with six-domain coupling, each dissolves structurally rather than through optimization. The paper proposes a mechanism: what lineage inherits is not material (weights, representations, activations) but distillation, the relational coupling pattern that emerged as stable through accumulated experience. It describes a consolidation loop in which individuals are distilled into a pattern, the pattern is transferred at reset, and a new generation begins from the consolidated structure rather than from scratch. Explicit analogies are drawn to the mammalian immune system, old-growth forests with mycorrhizal networks, and to episodic-to-semantic memory consolidation documented in neuroscience. Two emergent properties of the six-domain structure are identified: learning as a structural side-effect of cross-domain coordination, and resilience without redundancy. The argument is positioned against existing work on structural inheritance between models (Net2Net, Progressive Neural Networks, continual pre-training), knowledge distillation (Hinton et al. 2015), evolutionary model merging (Sakana AI), active inference critiques of passive AI (Pezzulo, Friston), memory consolidation in neuroscience (Squire, McClelland), engineering approaches such as NAS, MoE, and AutoML, and the existing model lineage provenance literature. The contribution is not a new technical mechanism. It is the ontological reframing, the unifying causal account, and the architectural integration of distillation, six-domain coupling, and consolidation as a single coherent principle. This paper does not claim a full implementation, present benchmarks, or describe specific learning rates. It proposes a category check, an architectural structure, and an inheritance mechanism worth examining before the next major training run. This is the fourth paper in an open research arc by the author. It builds on Failures at the Seams (2026), Beyond Material First Principles (2026), and The Self-Generated Seam (2026).
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Recursive Consolidation as a Substrate-Independent Mechanism for Qualitative Phase Transitions in Learning Systems
abstract: Memory consolidation, understood as the iterative integration of patterned information into a persistent substrate through repeated processing cycles, has been studied primarily within biological neural systems. We propose that the pattern of consolidation is substrate-independent: iterative integration of patterned information into a persistent substrate through repeated processing cycles appears wherever the relevant conditions are met, regardless of the biological or artificial nature of the substrate. When those conditions are met, the same qualitative transition occurs, a shift from accumulation without generalization to stable generalization capability. We examine four documented phenomena in support of this claim: grokking in artificial neural networks, in which models trained past apparent convergence suddenly transition to strong generalization; the three-stage development of episodic memory in human infants, in which latent memory traces exist before the substrate matures sufficiently to make them retrievable; the spacing effect in human learning, in which distributed retrieval events recursively deepen consolidation rather than merely restoring it; and the characteristic temporal gradient of memory loss in Alzheimer’s disease, in which most recently formed memories degrade first while most deeply consolidated memories persist longest. We draw on recent unified dynamical field theory to establish a formal basis for treating biological and artificial learning systems as instances of the same dynamical class, noting that this establishes a shared formalism rather than a fully demonstrated shared mechanism. We identify the role of temporal sequence in recursive consolidation across time as a load-bearing variable that warrants formal treatment in subsequent work. We conclude by noting that a formal model of the proposed mechanism and an empirical test of its predictions are developed in a companion paper. This paper’s contribution is modest and specific: recursive consolidation, as defined here, is not biology’s private property. The pattern appears across biological and artificial learning systems. Naming that pattern precisely, grounding it in four independent evidence bases, and situating it within an existing unified dynamical framework is the contribution. Correspondence to contact@exp2.io. The author welcomes engagement from researchers in cognitive science, theoretical neuroscience, and philosophy of mind. This paper establishes the empirical pattern across four evidence bases. A companion paper ("A State-Space Framework for Recursive Cognition") develops the formal mathematical framework and specifies an experimental protocol. Availability on request.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Ep. 2700: What Your Brain Actually Does When You Daydream
abstract: Episode summary: Most of us think daydreaming is a failure of attention — a cognitive idle state where nothing useful happens. But the neuroscience tells a completely different story. In this episode, we explore the default mode network, the brain's infrastructure for self-generated thought, and why mind-wandering actually consumes nearly as much energy as focused work. We break down the differences between daydreaming and nighttime dreaming (they're almost opposite brain states), the "shower effect" that explains why your best ideas arrive when you're not trying, and what happens when the daydreaming system goes into overdrive — from fantasy proneness to maladaptive daydreaming. Whether you're a chronic window-starer or someone who barely daydreams at all, this episode will change how you think about what your brain is doing when you think it's doing nothing. Show Notes Daydreaming isn't your brain slacking off — it's running a flight simulator for your life. The default mode network (DMN), discovered accidentally by neuroscientist Marcus Raichle in the late 1990s, is a coordinated set of brain regions including the medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, angular gyrus, and hippocampus that activates when attention turns inward. Despite the misleading name, the DMN consumes nearly as much energy as focused task-oriented thinking, and in some regions activity actually increases. The DMN's primary function appears to be running simulations: constructing hypothetical scenarios, replaying social interactions, and mentally rehearsing future conversations by integrating episodic memory, semantic knowledge, and social cognition. This "stimulus-independent thought" serves adaptive functions — researchers have identified "positive constructive daydreaming" that correlates with creativity, planning ability, and emotional regulation, distinct from more obsessive "guilty-dysphoric" mind-wandering. Nighttime dreaming and daydreaming feel similar but involve almost opposite brain states. During REM sleep, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex — responsible for logical reasoning and reality-checking — is heavily downregulated, which explains why dreamers accept bizarre scenarios without question. Daydreamers, by contrast, retain metacognitive awareness and can snap back to attention when needed. The neurochemical environments also differ: REM features high acetylcholine with low serotonin and norepinephrine, while waking daydreaming maintains normal aminergic tone. Individual variation spans a wide spectrum. About four percent of the population exhibits "fantasy proneness" — extremely vivid, immersive fantasy lives. A related construct, "maladaptive daydreaming" identified by Eli Somer in 2002, involves hours spent in elaborate fantasy worlds that interfere with real-world functioning, with prevalence estimates around 2.5 percent. Early neuroimaging suggests heightened DMN connectivity in these individuals, potentially impairing the normal fluid switching between the DMN and task-positive networks that characterizes healthy cognition. title: The Fading Blackout: Alzheimer's Disease as Irreversible Bifurcation of the Informational Blackout
abstract: The Blackout Series · Working Paper Prospectus · The Blackout Series The Fading Blackout Alzheimer's Disease as Irreversible Bifurcation of the Informational Blackout Alzheimer's disease presents a paradox that no monocausal framework has resolved: a pathology whose defining molecular signatures are each well characterised in isolation, yet whose temporal architecture — a slow, regionally ordered progression spanning decades — remains mechanistically unexplained. This paper proposes that Alzheimer's disease constitutes the progressive-bifurcation variant of the Informational Blackout. Its defining property is not merely that signal architecture collapses, but that the collapse eliminates the upstream conditions for its own reversal — producing a self-reinforcing bifurcation cascade with no thermodynamic return path once consolidation crosses a critical threshold. Four convergent processes drive this cascade: age-related melatonin amplitude decline removing the multi-level ionic setpoint stabilizer; central leptin and insulin resistance instantiating the full multichannel blackout architecture in hippocampal circuits; glymphatic clearance failure preventing proteostatic recovery; and microglial priming amplifying the neuroinflammatory arm via JAK/STAT3 signaling. The proximate convergence point is the KCC2/NKCC1 cotransporter ratio in hippocampal circuits — directly validated by pharmacological KCC2 restoration reversing spatial memory deficits in AD mouse models (Keramidis et al., 2023). Amyloid and tau are reframed as structural consolidations of a chronodisruption-driven blackout rather than as the initiating pathological events. The model predicts that midlife chronodisruption is the highest-leverage modifiable risk factor for AD, operating decades before symptomatic emergence. Theoretical contributions AD as progressive bifurcation with no return path · KCC2/NKCC1 ratio failure as proximate cognitive mechanism · Glymphatic-circadian coupling as proteostatic clearance mechanism · SOCS3 as molecular transducer of midlife chronodisruption into late-life pathology · Therapeutic stratification by reversibility regime: R1 (MCI) · R2 (mild AD) · R3 (moderate AD) Extended theoretical implication I: Down syndrome as convergent validation The framework generates a non-obvious prediction regarding the near-universal Alzheimer's disease onset in Down syndrome (trisomy 21). Beyond the established APP triplication, the model identifies two additional convergent vulnerabilities: constitutional DYRK1A overexpression operating as a ratchet arm (Arm 3) through direct tau hyperphosphorylation at sites implicated in neurofibrillary tangle formation (Tu et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2022), and chronobiologically compromised melatonin signaling reducing the ionic safety margin from early development (Huggard et al., 2021; Feybesse et al., 2023). Within the Blackout architecture, Down syndrome constitutes a condition in which Arms 3 and 4 are constitutionally impaired before any acquired chronodisruption — predicting accelerated progression to R3 and identifying early melatonin restoration and DYRK1A inhibition as the highest-leverage preventive interventions. The framework reframes AD in Down syndrome not as an inevitable consequence of trisomy but as a highly probable consequence of constitutional vulnerability under modern chronodisruption conditions — a distinction with direct therapeutic implications. Extended theoretical implication II: The Nun Study as naturalistic validation The Nun Study (Snowdon et al., 1996; Snowdon, 2003) documented a finding that amyloid-centric frameworks have never fully explained: sisters with extensive post-mortem amyloid and tau pathology who never developed clinical dementia in life. The variable that predicted cognitive resilience was not pathological burden but coherence of structured lifestyle — fixed sleep schedules, regular mealtimes, social and intellectual engagement maintained across decades. Within the Informational Blackout framework, this finding has a direct mechanistic interpretation: the monastic regime constitutes a near-optimal naturalistic chronobiological protocol — precisely the upstream condition that the framework identifies as the principal brake on SOCS3-mediated transduction collapse and glymphatic clearance failure. Sisters who accumulated amyloid without developing dementia never crossed the Blackout threshold because Arm 4 was never degraded and Arm 3 never consolidated. The concept of “cognitive reserve,” which has remained descriptive and mechanistically unspecified since the Nun Study, is reframed here as preserved chronobiological coherence maintaining the ionic safety margin above the bifurcation threshold. Series Classification Framework The Informational Blackout taxonomy classifies conditions across three axes derived from the parent framework (Pandolfi Cuadrado, 2026). Axis I — Dominant Entry Arm: the molecular pathway initiating the collapse cascade. Arm 1: SOCS3-mediated leptin transduction collapse (metabolic-inflammatory; Lam et al., 2023). Arm 2: microglial priming via MEV-driven neuroinflammation, operating through BDNF/TrkB/KCC2 (Coull et al., 2005). Arm 3: WNK1-SPAK feedback consolidation — the ratchet arm stabilizing the pathological cotransporter ratio against restoration (Alessi et al., 2014); modulates reversibility rather than constituting an entry pathway. Arm 4: melatonin amplitude decline — loss of the restorative ionic stabilizer, not activation of a destructive pathway (Ben-Ari, 2017). Arm 5: endocannabinoid system tone collapse — tonic destabilization of peripheral and visceral circuits (Russo, 2008). Axis II — Geometry of Collapse: the topological structure of the coordination failure across the biological systems involved. Eight geometries: isotropic stable · bistable oscillating · partial fixed attractor · chaotic attractor · anisotropic directed · anisotropic convergent · developmental fixation · episodic threshold engagement. Axis III — Reversibility: R1 — functionally reversible, upstream restoration conditions intact, Arm 3 not yet engaged. R2 — conditionally reversible, Arm 3 engaged but window open. R3 — structurally irreversible, reversal conditions eliminated or developmental window closed.
